M5|baseline|run1.question: What do papers in this collection use refinement types for?
M5|baseline|run1.answer:
The excerpts say refinement types are used for several related purposes:

- **To express and check program properties/policies.** One paper says base types are refined with predicates: “types include refined base types and function types” and “a refinement predicate over the program variables and a special value variable ν” [DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13]. It also notes these are used to “specify policies in data-centric applications” [DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13].

- **For program synthesis.** The PLDI paper explicitly studies “Program Synthesis from Polymorphic Refinement Types” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.18]. It says, “Our work is the first to leverage general decidable refinement types for synthesis” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.16].

- **To guide synthesis by restricting the search space and inferring conditions.** The same paper says the system uses refinement information to “restrict the search space” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.16], and gives an example where the goal refinement “can immediately discard the candidate y” and “leads to the abduction of the branch condition y ≤x” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.5].

- **To specify more expressive properties, including abstract refinements.** It says, “extending the type system with abstract refinements allows us to express a wider class of properties” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.5].

So, from these excerpts, refinement types are used to **specify policies/properties, support type checking, and enable or guide program synthesis** [DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13; DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.16; DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.5].

M5|agent_v1|run1.question: What do papers in this collection use refinement types for?
M5|agent_v1|run1.answer:
From the excerpts, refinement types are used for several related purposes:

1. **Program synthesis**
   - One paper says: “We present a method for synthesizing recursive functions that provably satisfy a given specification in the form of a polymorphic refinement type” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.1].
   - It also says refinement types provide “a unique combination of expressive power and decidability, which enables automatic verification—and hence synthesis—of nontrivial programs” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.1].

2. **Specifying program behavior and properties**
   - The synthesis paper says “a type-based specification for a program can often be effectively decomposed into independent specifications for its components” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.1].
   - It further notes that “refinement types are effective for specifying programs that manipulate data structures with nontrivial universal and inductive invariants” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.5].

3. **Expressing security policies / information-flow control**
   - In the information-flow paper, refinement terms are used inside types: “λL distinguishes between program terms t and refinement terms r, used inside types” [DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13].
   - The excerpt also says the authors “use them to specify policies in data-centric applications” [DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13].

4. **Type checking / inference with logical constraints**
   - The synthesis paper describes “a new algorithm for refinement type checking, which supports specification decomposition” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.1].
   - Another excerpt shows refinement constraints being solved and turned into Horn constraints, indicating they are used as part of the type-checking/inference machinery [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.11].

5. **Extending expressiveness via abstract refinements**
   - The paper says “extending the type system with abstract refinements allows us to express a wider class of properties” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.5].

So, based on these excerpts, papers in this collection use refinement types mainly for **synthesizing programs**, **specifying and verifying program properties**, and **expressing security/policy constraints**, especially where those properties involve **data structures, invariants, and information flow**.

Extended Version
Nadia Polikarpova Ivan Kuraj Armando Solar-Lezama
MIT CSAIL, USA
{polikarn,ivanko,asolar}@csail.mit.edu
Abstract
We present a method for synthesizing recursive functions
that provably satisfy a given specification in the form of a
polymorphic refinement type. We observe that such speci-
fications are particularly suitable for program synthesis for
two reasons. First, they offer a unique combination of ex-
pressive power and decidability, which enables automatic
verification—and hence synthesis—of nontrivial programs.
Second, a type-based specification for a program can often
be effectively decomposed into independent specifications
for its components, causing the synthesizer to consider fewer
component combinations and leading to a combinatorial re-
duction in the size of the search space. At the core of our
synthesis procedure is a new algorithm for refinement type
checking, which supports specification decomposition.
We have evaluated our prototype implementation on a
large set of synthesis problems and found that it exceeds
the state of the art in terms of both scalability and usability.
The tool was able to synthesize more complex programs than
those reported in prior work (several sorting algorithms and
operations on balanced search trees), as well as most of the

The excerpts show two main uses of refinement types in these papers:

1. **Program synthesis**
   - The paper says it presents “a method for synthesizing recursive functions that provably satisfy a given specification in the form of a polymorphic refinement type” and that “such specifications are particularly suitable for program synthesis” because they combine “expressive power and decidability” and can be “effectively decomposed” for synthesis [source p.1].
   - It also says the work is about “Program Synthesis from Polymorphic Refinement Types” and that it uses refinement types to reduce the search space by decomposing specifications [source p.1].

2. **Specifying and verifying properties/policies of programs**
   - One excerpt explains that in λL, “types include refined base types and function types,” where a refined base type has “a refinement predicate” over program variables and a value variable [source p.13].
   - The paper further notes that “we use them to specify policies in data-centric applications” [source p.13].
   - Another excerpt says refinement types are “effective for specifying programs that manipulate data structures with nontrivial universal and inductive invariants” [source p.5].

So, from these excerpts, refinement types are used for **specifying program properties, policies, and invariants**, and as a basis for **automatic program synthesis and verification** [source p.1; source p.5; source p.13].

Program Synthesis from Polymorphic Refinement Types
Extended Version
Nadia Polikarpova Ivan Kuraj Armando Solar-Lezama
MIT CSAIL, USA
{polikarn,ivanko,asolar}@csail.mit.edu
Abstract
We present a method for synthesizing recursive functions
that provably satisfy a given specification in the form of a
polymorphic refinement type. We observe that such speci-
fications are particularly suitable for program synthesis for
two reasons. First, they offer a unique combination of ex-
pressive power and decidability, which enables automatic
verification—and hence synthesis—of nontrivial programs.
Second, a type-based specification for a program can often
be effectively decomposed into independent specifications
for its components, causing the synthesizer to consider fewer
component combinations and leading to a combinatorial re-
duction in the size of the search space. At the core of our
synthesis procedure is a new algorithm for refinement type
checking, which supports specification decomposition.
We have evaluated our prototype implementation on a
large set of synthesis problems and found that it exceeds
the state of the art in terms of both scalability and usability.
The tool was able to synthesize more complex programs than
those reported in prior work (several sorting algorithms and
operations on balanced search trees), as well as most of the

M5|agent_v2|run1.question: What do papers in this collection use refinement types for?
M5|agent_v2|run1.answer:
From the excerpts, the papers use refinement types for several related purposes:

- **To specify programs and program properties more precisely.** One paper says, “Using refinement types, we were able to express 3 out of 3, 10, 5, and 7 of their most complex benchmarks” and that “refinement types are concise and intuitive” for some tasks like “insertion into a binary search tree” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.15].

- **As an interface for program synthesis.** The same paper says, “Using refinement types as an interface to synthesis raises the question of their expressiveness” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.5], and elsewhere says, “Our work is the first to leverage general decidable refinement types for synthesis” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.16].

- **To capture data-structure invariants and other semantic properties.** It states that “refinement types are effective for specifying programs that manipulate data structures with nontrivial universal and inductive invariants” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.5]. It also mentions extending the type system with abstract refinements “to express a wider class of properties” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.5].

- **To support modular type checking and checking of applications/branching terms.** The paper says the system uses “top-down propagation of over-approximate type information” and a “novel liquid abduction rule” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.2]. It further says “The application rules APPFO and AppHO are the core of the round-trip type system” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.9].

- **To control information flow / specify security policies.** Another excerpt from Liquid Information Flow Control says the system has “refined base types” and that “we use them to specify policies in data-centric applications” [DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13].

What the excerpts do **not** provide is a single unified statement of all uses across the whole collection; they do, however, clearly show refinement types being used for **specification, synthesis, modular checking, and information-flow/security policies** [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.2; DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.5; DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13].

M5|baseline|run2.question: What do papers in this collection use refinement types for?
M5|baseline|run2.answer:
The excerpts say the papers use refinement types for several related purposes:

- **To specify and reason about programs with logical properties.** One paper says refinement types are used to distinguish program terms from refinement terms, and that in refined base types, “`r` is a refinement predicate over the program variables and a special value variable `ν`” [DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13].

- **To guide program synthesis.** The synthesis paper explicitly says, “Our work is the first to leverage general decidable refinement types for synthesis” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.16]. It also says the system “integrate[s] their ideas with bidirectional type checking” and uses refinement types to restrict the search space [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.17].

- **To express program specifications, especially invariants and policies.** The paper states that “we use them to specify policies in data-centric applications” [DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13], and that refinement types are “effective for specifying programs that manipulate data structures with nontrivial universal and inductive invariants” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.5].

- **To support abstraction and inference over logical constraints.** The synthesis paper describes “refinement type inference” and says SYNQUID combines it with “predicate abstraction” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.16], and elsewhere notes “greatest-fixpoint predicate abstraction” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.17].

In short, from these excerpts, refinement types are used for **specifying properties of programs, encoding policies and invariants, and enabling synthesis and type-directed inference** [DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13; DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.16; DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.5].

M5|agent_v1|run2.question: What do papers in this collection use refinement types for?
M5|agent_v1|run2.answer:
The excerpts show refinement types being used for several related purposes:

1. **To specify and synthesize programs**
   - “we propose a new type checking mechanism for refinement types, which we dub local liquid type checking” and it is part of “Program Synthesis from Polymorphic Refinement Types” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.2].
   - The paper says refinement types are used as “an interface to synthesis” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.5].

2. **To express program properties and invariants**
   - “Using refinement types, we were able to express 3 out of 3, 10, 5, and 7 of their most complex benchmarks” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.15].
   - It also says refinement types are “effective for specifying programs that manipulate data structures with nontrivial universal and inductive invariants” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.5].

3. **To help with modular type checking and local error detection**
   - The paper says the mechanism aims to “support decomposing a specification into independent requirements for their sub-terms” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.2].
   - It also says the type checking mechanism “achieves locality” and can “detect type errors locally” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.6].

4. **To aid synthesis and code completion**
   - It notes that “type information has also proved extremely useful for code completion” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.17].
   - It also mentions “hole driven development” systems that “leverage a rich type system to aid development” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.17].

5. **To specify policies in data-centric applications**
   - The λL paper says the implementation “supports dependent function types” and “we use them to specify policies in data-centric applications” [DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13].

So, from these excerpts, refinement types are used for **specifying program behavior and invariants, enabling synthesis, supporting modular/local type checking, and expressing policies**.

M5|baseline_matched|run2.question: What do papers in this collection use refinement types for?
M5|baseline_matched|run2.answer:
The excerpts say refinement types are used mainly for **specification, verification, and synthesis** of programs.

- The synthesis paper says it presents “**a method for synthesizing recursive functions that provably satisfy a given specification in the form of a polymorphic refinement type**” and that refinement types “**offer a unique combination of expressive power and decidability, which enables automatic verification—and hence synthesis—of nontrivial programs**” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.1].
- It also says the type system is used for “**specification decomposition**” in synthesis [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.1].
- The overview describes refinement types as part of a framework that uses them for program specifications: “**We equip the language with general decidable refinement types**” and “**Base types can be combined into dependent function types**” to express properties of programs [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.3].
- The liquid information flow paper shows another use: refinement types are used to describe and reason about program properties via labels and predicates inside types, noting that “**λL distinguishes between program terms t and refinement terms r, used inside types**” and that “**r is a refinement predicate over the program variables and a special value variable ν**” [DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13].

So, from these excerpts, refinement types are used to **express program specifications and policies, support automatic verification, and enable program synthesis** [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.1; DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.3; DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13].

Abstract
We present a method for synthesizing recursive functions

polymorphic refinement type. We observe that such speci-

two reasons. First, they offer a unique combination of ex-
pressive power and decidability, which enables automatic
verification—and hence synthesis—of nontrivial programs.

be effectively decomposed into independent specifications

component combinations and leading to a combinatorial re-
duction in the size of the search space. At the core of our
synthesis procedure is a new algorithm for refinement type
checking, which supports specification decomposition.
We have evaluated our prototype implementation on a
large set of synthesis problems and found that it exceeds
the state of the art in terms of both scalability and usability.
The tool was able to synthesize more complex programs than
those reported in prior work (several sorting algorithms and
operations on balanced search trees), as well as most of the
ben

can handle the majority of its competitors’ most challenging
benchmarks, taking a similar or shorter amount of time. In ad-
dition, compared with the example-based tools, SYNQUID’s
specifications are usually more concise and the generated so-
lutions are provably correct; compared with the tools based on
Hoare-style reasoning, SYNQUID can verify (and thus synthe-
size) more complex programs thanks to automatic refinement
inference.

conditionals, algebraic datatypes, pattern matching, paramet-

The excerpts show two main uses of refinement types in this collection:

1. **Program synthesis / specification of programs**
   - The PLDI paper says it is about “**Program Synthesis from Polymorphic Refinement Types**” and explains that “**Using refinement types, we were able to express 3 out of 3, 10, 5, and 7 of their most complex benchmarks**” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.15].
   - It also notes that “**refinement types are concise and intuitive**” for some tasks [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.15], and that “**our work is the first to leverage general decidable refinement types for synthesis**” [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.16].

2. **Information flow control / security policies**
   - The Journals excerpt says λL has “**refined base types**” where “**r is a refinement predicate**” and that dependent function types are used “**to specify policies in data-centric applications**” [DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13].
   - The paper “Liquid Information Flow Control” and its benchmark show refinement types used to encode confidentiality constraints, e.g. types annotated with policies like `<{True}> <{False}>` and `<{¬(_0 in (paperConflicts ds)[[pid]])}> <{False}>` [DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.40].

So, from these excerpts, papers in this collection use refinement types for **synthesizing programs from specifications** and for **expressing/enforcing information-flow security policies** [DBLP_conf_pldi_PolikarpovaKS16 p.16; DBLP_journals_corr_PolikarpovaYIS16 p.13].

M7|baseline|run1.answer:
Stitch differs from DreamCoder mainly in **how it searches for abstractions and how it is used with rewrite systems**.

- DreamCoder “**learns libraries iteratively: the system is initialized with a low-level DSL, and then alternates between synthesizing programs … and updating the library of abstractions**” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.18].
- Stitch instead “**synthesizes the maximally-compressive abstraction for a corpus of programs through a branch-and-bound top-down search, computing an upper bound on the compression of any partially-constructed abstraction to guide and prune the search**” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.28].

The excerpt also says Stitch is designed to be **efficient**, while babble is more expressive; in particular, “**Stitch focuses primarily on efficient library learning through a parallel anytime branch-and-bound algorithm**” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.28].

Compared with DreamCoder, Stitch is presented as much faster: “**Stitch is 1,000-10,000x faster than DreamCoder**” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.28], and the paper reports that Stitch usually matches or exceeds DreamCoder’s library quality while using far less compute: “**Stitch learns libraries which usually match or exceed the baseline in quality … while improving the resource efficiency in terms of memory usage and runtime by 2 and 3-4 orders of magnitude compared to the baseline**” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.17].

So, based on the excerpts, DreamCoder learns libraries by an iterative synthesize-and-update loop, while Stitch learns them by direct top-down branch-and-bound search for maximally compressive abstractions, emphasizing efficiency.

M7|agent_v2|run1.question: How does Stitch's approach to library learning differ from DreamCoder's?
M7|agent_v2|run1.answer:
Stitch differs from DreamCoder in both how it learns abstractions and how it is positioned computationally.

- DreamCoder is described as an iterative deductive learner: “the system is initialized with a low-level DSL, and then alternates between synthesizing programs … and updating the library of abstractions available to the synthesizer” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.18].
- Stitch instead is presented as a top-down synthesis method: “Stitch synthesizes the maximally-compressive abstraction for a corpus of programs through a branch-and-bound top-down search, computing an upper bound on the compression of any partially-constructed abstraction to guide and prune the search” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.28].

The excerpt also contrasts their goals and strengths:
- “Stitch focuses primarily on efficient library learning through a parallel anytime branch-and-bound algorithm,” whereas DreamCoder is the baseline deductive system [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.28].
- On efficiency, “Stitch is 1,000-10,000x faster than DreamCoder” and uses “more than 2 orders of magnitude less memory” in the reported experiments [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.28; DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.20].
- On quality, “Stitch generally learns libraries of comparable and often greater quality than DreamCoder when matching the number of abstractions learned by the latter” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.19].

A limitation noted in the excerpt is that “Stitch cannot learn higher-order abstractions” in the list domain [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.19], while DreamCoder can handle some higher-order functionality via its deductive/version-space machinery [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.25].

M7|baseline|run2.question: How does Stitch's approach to library learning differ from DreamCoder's?
M7|baseline|run2.answer:
Stitch differs from DreamCoder in both method and emphasis.

- DreamCoder “learns libraries iteratively”: “the system is initialized with a low-level DSL, and then alternates between synthesizing programs … and updating the library of abstractions available to the synthesizer” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.18].
- Stitch instead uses “a branch-and-bound top-down search” and “comput[es] an upper bound on the compression of any partially-constructed abstraction to guide and prune the search” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.28].
- The paper also contrasts their goals: “Stitch aims to be efficient while babble aims to be expressive,” and in the comparison with DreamCoder it reports that Stitch is “1,000-10,000x faster than DreamCoder” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.28].
- A further distinction is that DreamCoder uses “a probabilistic Bayesian objective” for candidate abstractions, while “Stitch, on the other hand, effectively judges compression quality via a cost” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.25].

So, based on the excerpts, DreamCoder learns libraries through iterative synthesis plus updating, whereas Stitch learns them through a top-down, branch-and-bound compression search designed for efficiency.

M7|agent_v1|run2.answer:
Stitch differs from DreamCoder in that it uses a **top-down synthesis / branch-and-bound search** for library learning, while DreamCoder uses an **iterative deductive** process.

The paper says Stitch “**synthesizes the maximally-compressive abstraction for a corpus of programs through a branch-and-bound top-down search**” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.28]. By contrast, “**DreamCoder learns libraries iteratively: the system is initialized with a low-level DSL, and then alternates between synthesizing programs ... and updating the library of abstractions available to the synthesizer**” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.18].

The excerpt also emphasizes that Stitch is designed to be more efficient: “**Stitch is 1,000-10,000x faster than DreamCoder**” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.28], and in the experiments “**Stitch takes tens of milliseconds to discover abstractions across all five domains**” while using “**more than 2 orders of magnitude less memory**” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.20].

So, in short: DreamCoder learns libraries by **iterating synthesis and updating its DSL/library**, whereas Stitch learns by **directly searching for compressive abstractions top-down**, with a strong focus on speed and resource efficiency [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.18][DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.28][DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.20].

M7|baseline_matched|run2.answer:
Stitch differs from DreamCoder in how it searches for abstractions and in its efficiency.

- DreamCoder “learns libraries iteratively”: “the system is initialized with a low-level DSL, and then alternates between synthesizing programs … that solve a training corpus of inductive tasks and updating the library of abstractions available to the synthesizer” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.18].

So, from these excerpts, DreamCoder uses iterative synthesis plus library updating, while Stitch uses a top-down branch-and-bound search for compressive abstractions and is much more resource-efficient [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.18] [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.28].

M7|agent_v2|run2.question: How does Stitch's approach to library learning differ from DreamCoder's?
M7|agent_v2|run2.answer:
Stitch and DreamCoder differ in how they search for abstractions and how they use the corpus.

DreamCoder “learns libraries iteratively”: “the system is initialized with a low-level DSL, and then alternates between synthesizing programs … that solve a training corpus of inductive tasks and updating the library of abstractions available to the synthesizer” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.18]. By contrast, Stitch is described as a “corpus-guided top-down library learning tool” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.3], and “the top-down search algorithm described above yields a single abstraction,” which can then be run “for multiple iterations on a corpus of programs to build up an entire library of abstractions” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.6].

The paper also emphasizes a performance difference: Stitch “learns comparably compressive libraries with 2 orders of magnitude less memory and 3-4 orders of magnitude less time compared to the state-of-the-art deductive algorithm of Ellis et al. 2021” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.29], and in the comparison with DreamCoder, “Stitch takes tens of milliseconds to discover abstractions across all five domains—achieving a 3-4 order of magnitude speed-up over DreamCoder—while also requiring more than 2 orders of magnitude less memory” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.20].

So, from these excerpts, the main difference is that DreamCoder uses an iterative synthesize-and-update loop, while Stitch uses corpus-guided top-down search to discover abstractions, typically with much lower time and memory use [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.18; p.6; p.20; p.29].

M7|baseline_matched_v2|run2.answer:
Stitch differs from DreamCoder in that it learns libraries with a **top-down search over abstractions directly from a corpus**, rather than DreamCoder’s **iterative synthesize-and-update loop**.

The excerpt says Stitch “**builds abstractions directly from initial DSL primitives, using syntactic pattern matching of intermediate abstractions to intelligently prune the search space**” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.1]. In contrast, “**DreamCoder learns libraries iteratively: the system is initialized with a low-level DSL, and then alternates between synthesizing programs ... and updating the library of abstractions available to the synthesizer**” [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.18].

The excerpts also emphasize a goal difference: “**Stitch focuses primarily on efficient library learning through a parallel anytime branch-and-bound algorithm**,” whereas “**babble focuses primarily on expressive library learning**” and DreamCoder is a deductive baseline in these comparisons [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.28]. More directly, Stitch “**aims to be efficient**” and “**is 1,000-10,000x faster than DreamCoder**” on DreamCoder’s benchmarks [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.28].

So, in short: DreamCoder learns libraries by iterating synthesis and abstraction updates, while Stitch learns abstractions more directly with top-down, corpus-guided search and pruning [DBLP_journals_pacmpl_BowersOWGTES23 p.1; p.18].

Abstract
Physical products are often complex assemblies combin-
ing a multitude of 3D parts modeled in computer-aided de-
sign (CAD) software. CAD designers build up these assem-
blies by aligning individual parts to one another using con-
straints called joints. In this paper we introduce JoinABLe,
a learning-based method that assembles parts together to
form joints. JoinABLe uses the weak supervision available
in standard parametric CAD files without the help of object
class labels or human guidance. Our results show that by
making network predictions over a graph representation of
solid models we can outperform multiple baseline methods
with an accuracy (79.53%) that approaches human perfor-
mance (80%). Finally, to support future research we release
the Fusion 360 Gallery assembly dataset, containing as-
semblies with rich information on joints, contact surfaces,
holes, and the underlying assembly graph structure.

1 INTRODUCTION
The manufactured objects that surround us in everyday life are
represented programmatically in computer-aided design (CAD) soft-
ware as a sequence of 2D and 3D modeling operations. Parametric
CAD files contain programmatic information that is critical for doc-
umenting design intent, maintaining editablity, and compatibility
with downstream simulation and manufacturing. Embedded within
these designs is the knowledge of domain experts who precisely
define a sequence of modeling operations to form 3D shapes. We
believe having access to a real-world collection of human design
sequences, and the ability to execute them, is critical for future
advances in CAD that leverage learning-based approaches.
Learning-based approaches show great potential, both for solving
existing problems such as reverse engineering [Buonamici et al.
2018], and for providing entirely new kinds of functionality which
would be unimaginable using traditional techniques. Recent ad-
vances in neural networks have spurred new interest in data driven
approaches to generating CAD programs, tackling both the forward
problem of 3D shape generation [Jones et al. 2020; Li et al. 2020b;
Mo et al. 2019a] and the inverse problem of recovering CAD pro-

7.1 Limitations
Our dataset contains only designs created using sketch and extrude
rather than the full array of CAD modeling operations. Short con-
struction sequences make up a sizable portion of the data: 3267/8625
(38%) of designs have only a single extrude operation. From the
single extrude designs, some exhibit more complexity: 347 have >1
sketch profile resulting in ≥1 bodies from a single extrude opera-
tion, and 998 have ≥8 sketch curves. Other designs are washers,
pegs, and plates, common in mechanical CAD assemblies. We avoid
filtering simple designs to ensure the dataset is representative of
user-designed CAD. Spline curves represent 4% of curves in the
dataset and are not currently supported by our high-level DSL,
however they can be reconstructed via the reconstruct_curve()
command (Section A.2.1).
The success of the rand agent demonstrates that short construc-
tion sequences can be solved by a naive approach. This is due to
several factors: 1) our action representation that uses B-Rep faces,
2) our search procedure discarding invalid actions, and 3) designs
in the dataset with a low number of planar faces and extrude steps.
For example, a washer has four B-Rep faces (planar-top, cylinder-

tested beyond mechanical CAD data. Finally, our network
does not leverage geometric loss terms that may help with
avoiding undesirable overlap between parts and generalize
to predicting other joint parameters.
7. Conclusion
Our long-term motivation is to enable assembly-aware
design tools, capable of suggesting and automatically plac-
ing parts. Such a system could enable greater reuse of ex-
isting physical components in new designs and potentially
reduce the cost and environmental impact associated with
manufacturing and associated supply chains [29]. Under-
standing how parts are assembled is also critical for robotic
assembly and disassembly. CAD-informed robotic disas-
sembly systems may enhance our ability to reuse and recy-
cle components [8, 35, 41, 45]. In this work we have begun
the first steps to address these challenges by learning the
bottom-up assembly of parametric CAD joints. Our results
show the promise of learning-based methods to approach
the performance of human CAD experts, and with the publi-
cation of our dataset we hope to further aid future research.

The Fusion 360 Gallery paper contributes a **dataset, DSL, and reconstruction environment** for learning from CAD designs. It says the paper presents “**the Fusion 360 Gallery, consisting of a simple language with just the sketch and extrude modeling operations, and a dataset of 8,625 human design seq**” [DBLP_journals_tog_WillisPLCDLSM21 p.1]. It also states that “**we provide an open source environment, called the Fusion 360 Gym, for standardizing the CAD reconstruction task for learning-based approaches**” [DBLP_journals_tog_WillisPLCDLSM21 p.6]. The dataset is described as “**8,625 designs produced by users of the CAD software Autodesk Fusion 360**” [DBLP_journals_tog_WillisPLCDLSM21 p.4].

JoinABLe contributes a **learning-based method for assembling CAD parts into joints** and a related assembly dataset. Its abstract says, “**we introduce JoinABLe, a learning-based method that assembles parts together to form joints**” [DBLP_conf_cvpr_WillisJCT0GSTLS22 p.1]. It further says JoinABLe “**uses the weak supervision available in standard parametric CAD files without the help of object class labels or human guidance**” [DBLP_conf_cvpr_WillisJCT0GSTLS22 p.1]. For resources, it says they “**release the Fusion 360 Gallery assembly dataset, containing assemblies with rich information on joints, contact surfaces, holes, and the underlying assembly graph structure**” [DBLP_conf_cvpr_WillisJCT0GSTLS22 p.1].

So, in short: Fusion 360 Gallery provides the **data and environment for CAD reconstruction from human design sequences**, while JoinABLe provides a **method and assembly dataset for learning how CAD parts connect via joints** [DBLP_journals_tog_WillisPLCDLSM21 p.6; DBLP_conf_cvpr_WillisJCT0GSTLS22 p.1].

A.1. Dataset
The Fusion 360 Gallery assembly dataset consists of
two inter-related sets of data with assembly data and joint
data. The data and supporting code are publicly available on
GitHub2 with a license allowing non-commercial research.
We now outline related datasets, data processing steps, doc-
umentation, and statistics about the dataset.
A.1.1 Related Datasets
The ABC dataset [30] provides 1 million CAD assemblies
in the B-Rep format, containing valuable analytic repre-
sentations of surfaces and curves. However, each assem-
bly contains individual part files positioned in global space
without the critical joint information describing how parts
are connected and constrained together. Other datasets pro-
viding designs in B-Rep format only include part geometry
and lack assembly data entirely [25, 31, 62, 63].
Recently a number of datasets have extended existing
3D shape datasets, such as ShapeNet [7] and PartNet [47],
with additional human annotated labels for part mobil-
ity [21, 58, 65, 68]. The resulting synthetic assemblies have
joint type and range of motion information included. Our
dataset differs from these datasests in several ways:
1. We provide CAD assemblies that are more represen-
tative of real world design, including detailed design
such as fasteners.
2. Joint connectivity and component hierarchy are de-
fined by the designers

esentations via contacts, joints, or the designer-
defined assembly tree.
2. We provide assembly metadata listing the contact sur-
faces, hole types, materials, and various user specified
tags for each design.
3. We consolidate joints across the dataset, meaning that
for two given parts in our joint data we list all known
ground truth joints between them. This avoids pre-
senting the network with contradictory labels during
training, where multiple different versions of a pos-
itively labelled joint configuration could exist across
data samples.
4. We provide a ‘clean’ test and validation set for joint
prediction by removing potential positive unlabeled
samples.
Ultimately we believe both datasets will be helpful to cross-
validate using designs created in different CAD software
and increase the robustness of learning-based methods. Fu-
ture updates to the AutoMate dataset may include a number
of the capabilities listed above.

M9|agent_v1|run2.answer:
The excerpts say the **Fusion 360 Gallery** paper contributes a **dataset and environment for programmatic CAD reconstruction / construction from human design sequences**. It presents “**the Fusion 360 Gallery, consisting of a simple language with just the sketch and extrude modeling operations, and a dataset of 8,625 human design seq**” [DBLP_journals_tog_WillisPLCDLSM21 p.1], and further states that “**we provide an open source environment, called the Fusion 360 Gym, for standardizing the CAD reconstruction task for learning-based approaches**” [DBLP_journals_tog_WillisPLCDLSM21 p.6]. The paper also says the benchmark has “**a training set of 6,900 designs and a test set of 1,725 designs**” [DBLP_journals_tog_WillisPLCDLSM21 p.2].

The **JoinABLe** paper contributes a **learning-based method for assembling CAD parts using weak supervision from parametric CAD files**, plus a dataset focused on assemblies and joints. It says, “**we introduce JoinABLe, a learning-based method that assembles parts together to form joints**” [DBLP_conf_cvpr_WillisJCT0GSTLS22 p.1], and that it “**uses the weak supervision available in standard parametric CAD files without the help of object class labels or human guidance**” [DBLP_conf_cvpr_WillisJCT0GSTLS22 p.1]. It also says they “**release the Fusion 360 Gallery assembly dataset, containing assemblies with rich information on joints, contact surfaces, holes, and the underlying assembly graph structure**” [DBLP_conf_cvpr_WillisJCT0GSTLS22 p.1].

In short:
- **Fusion 360 Gallery**: a **CAD reconstruction dataset + environment** for learning from human design sequences [DBLP_journals_tog_WillisPLCDLSM21 p.1][DBLP_journals_tog_WillisPLCDLSM21 p.6].
- **JoinABLe**: a **bottom-up assembly learning method** for learning joints from CAD assemblies using weak supervision [DBLP_conf_cvpr_WillisJCT0GSTLS22 p.1][DBLP_conf_cvpr_WillisJCT0GSTLS22 p.2].

From the excerpts, the two papers contribute different resources and learning setups:

- **Fusion 360 Gallery** contributes a **dataset and environment for programmatic CAD reconstruction** from human designs.
